desc:
The median of a list is its middle value after sorting; for an even length it is the average of the two middle values. To stay with integers, return twice the median: the sum of the two middle sorted values for an even length, or the middle value counted twice for an odd length.

You are not required to sort the whole array. A selection algorithm such as quickselect finds a middle value in expected linear time.

nums = [7, 1, 5]        sorted 1 5 7      median 5      answer 10
nums = [4, 9, 1, 2]     sorted 1 2 4 9    median 3      answer 6
hints: Sorting gives the answer in O(n log n). The question only needs the one or two middle positions, not a full order.
Choose a pivot and split the values into smaller, equal and larger groups. Which group contains the position you are looking for?
Quickselect: keep looking for index n // 2 (and, for even n, n // 2 - 1) and discard the groups that cannot contain it.
editorial: With zero-based sorted positions, the lower middle is at (n - 1) // 2 and the upper middle at n // 2. For odd n these are the same position, so adding them yields exactly twice the median; for even n the sum is twice the average. One formula covers both cases.

Each position is found with quickselect: pick a random pivot, split into elements less than, equal to and greater than the pivot, and continue in the part that holds the target rank. The expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n). Using a three-way split keeps the algorithm fast on arrays with many equal values.
Plain sorting (O(n log n)) is perfectly acceptable at these sizes, but the selection version is the one interviewers usually ask for.
